children: Uganda is attempting to revive its dormant corporate bond market by pushing companies to use credit ratings, sinking funds and financial guarantees to win back investors attracted to safer, higher-yielding Treasury bonds and bills.

Uganda’s Capital Markets Authority (CMA) says that high returns on government securities have made corporate bonds less attractive to issuers and investors, as companies face higher borrowing costs to compete with the safer, high-yielding government instruments.“Elevated yields on government securities made corporate bonds less attractive to issuers and investors, as corporations faced higher borrowing costs to compete with the safer, high-yielding government instruments,” the regulator said last week in its latest annual report for 2025.“To stimulate issuance in the primary market, CMA continues to raise awareness among business owners and founders on the benefits of corporate bonds as an alternative source of market-based financing. Efforts also continue to lobby for a favourable tax regime. Furthermore, the CMA is promoting the use of tools such as guarantees, sinking funds and credit ratings to enhance investor confidence.”Independent credit ratings of potential issuers are changing the business of bond trading by giving institutional investors a reliable way of measuring risks.

A corporate bond is a debt security issued by companies to raise funds from the capital markets, where investors typically lend money to companies with the expectation of being repaid the principal with interest.
In the past, buying a corporate bond meant having to guess a company’s financial health, but rated companies face increasing pressure to practise greater financial transparency.

Companies secure bond repayments through sinking funds by setting aside specific cash reserves over time before the debt matures, while a third-party guarantee promises that debt obligations will be met even if the company hits a rough patch.

By combining transparent credit scores, dedicated sinking funds and protective guarantees, Uganda is rewriting its corporate bond market story by transforming it from a risky investment into a secure and reliable engine for long-term national development.“In line with Uganda’s Fourth National Development Plan (NDPIV), which emphasises the need for innovative financing mechanisms to drive the ten-fold growth strategy, the CMA is actively engaging entities, particularly state-owned enterprises (SOEs), to issue corporate bonds as a means of mobilising long-term capital for development,” CMA says.
During the year ended June 30, 2025, there was no activity in either the primary or secondary markets for corporate bonds in Uganda.

Yields on Treasury bonds in the primary market rose across all maturities during the financial year, reflecting the Bank of Uganda’s (BoU) tight monetary policy stance aimed at containing inflation, as well as increased government borrowing requirements to finance fiscal needs.“A high-interest-rate environment for Treasury securities can attract more investors to government debt, providing a stable and predictable investment option. This environment encourages businesses to prioritise efficiency and high-return projects, promoting better resource allocation,” CMA says.“However, high yields also indicate higher borrowing costs for the government as investors demand greater compensation for the risks of holding long-term fixed-income securities. Ongoing initiatives, such as the establishment of the Uganda Fixed Income Market Committee (UFIMC), aim to spur secondary market activity and facilitate appropriate pricing of risk in the fixed-income securities market.”At the close of the 2024/2025 financial year, 68.7 percent of assets under management (AUM) by collective investment schemes (CIS) was allocated to Government of Uganda bonds, and 9.3 percent to Government of Uganda Treasury bills.
A five-year trend analysis (2020/21–2024/25) shows a decline in allocations to corporate bonds, from 1.4 percent to 0.2 percent.

A bulk of assets under management by fund managers, at 80 percent, was allocated to government bonds in the 2024/2025 fiscal year, with 2.4 percent in Treasury bills and only 0.2 percent in corporate bonds.

Over the past ten years, government bond turnover on the secondary market has increased from Ush 3.5 trillion ($923.65 million) in the 2015/2016 financial year to Ush 73.8 trillion ($19.47 billion) in the 2024/2025 financial year.

So far, only nine companies have issued corporate bonds in Uganda since the inception of the market in 1998. These are the East African Development Bank (EADB), the Eastern and Southern African Trade and Development Bank — currently the Trade and Development Bank (TDB) — MTN, Uganda Telecom Ltd, Standard Chartered Bank, Housing Finance Bank Ltd, Stanbic Bank Uganda Ltd and Kakira Sugar Ltd.

However, since December 2013, when sugar manufacturer Kakira Sugar Ltd issued its Ush 76 billion ($20.05 million) corporate bond, Uganda’s capital markets have not witnessed any new corporate debt issuance.

In Kenya, several companies have collapsed in the past, while others have defaulted on their loan obligations in the corporate debt market, eliciting jitters among investors, particularly due to the lack of a clear compensation mechanism for bondholders.

In Kenya, the Treasury bond market remains dominant, accounting for about 99.98 percent of the debt market, with corporate bonds at only 0.02 percent, according to data from Kenya’s Capital Markets Authority (CMA) as at June 30, 2026.“This subdued performance of corporate bonds is attributed to ongoing investor preference for relatively higher-yielding and more liquid government instruments,” Kenya’s CMA says.
